A probability distribution describes uncertainty, but we do not observe it directly. We see only finite, noisy samples drawn from it. When we study an astronomical population, we have a limited set of measurements, each with its own uncertainty. Because our observations are limited and uncertain, our models and inferences carry uncertainty too. How do we extract reliable information about the distribution from such data?

The methods in later chapters depend on this. Linear regression (Chapters 4 and 5) estimates means, variances, and covariances from samples to determine the best model parameters and to quantify their uncertainties. In the M-\(\sigma\) relation between black hole mass and stellar velocity dispersion, we need the best-fit line, its confidence, and predictions for new observations.

Bayesian inference (Chapter 5) needs complete probability distributions over the parameters. This requires methods that separate measurement noise, the irreducible randomness in the data, from model uncertainty, our incomplete knowledge of the parameters. Section 3.8 calls these aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Model comparison depends on this distinction too.

The solution is to use summary statistics. Limited data rarely determine the full distribution, but summary statistics capture its main features, and we can estimate them from finite samples. Expectations give central tendencies, variances give scatter and measurement precision, and covariances give the relationships between observed quantities, which lets us build predictive models. We build these tools from the expectation operator and the moments of a distribution. We then study how they behave under transformations and how uncertainties combine when we average measurements, combine datasets, or propagate errors through calculations.

3.1 Moments of Distributions

Moments give a systematic way to describe a probability distribution. They support the parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification that machine learning needs.

For a random variable \(X\) with probability distribution \(p(x)\), we define the \(k\)th moment as \[\begin{aligned} \text{Discrete case:} \quad \mu_k &= \sum_x x^k p(x), \\ \text{Continuous case:} \quad \mu_k &= \int x^k p(x) \mathrm{d}x. \end{aligned}\]

We often write these expressions with the expectation operator \[ \mu_k = \mathbb{E}[x^k], \] where \(\mathbb{E}[\cdot]\) denotes the expectation, or average, of a quantity weighted by its probability distribution. We use this notation throughout the chapter.

For discrete variables, we sum over the possible values (finite or countably infinite), with \(p(x)\) the probability mass function. For continuous variables, we integrate over the range of possible values, with \(p(x)\) the probability density function. We need this distinction because a continuous variable has zero probability of taking any exact value, so we work with probability densities over intervals.

Each moment \(\mu_k\) weights the distribution by a higher power of \(x\), so each moment emphasizes different features of its shape.

The first moment (\(k=1\)) is the mean or expected value \[ \mu_1 = \mathbb{E}[x] = \int x p(x) \mathrm{d}x. \] It gives the center or typical value of the distribution, which is the basis for parameter estimation in linear regression. Recall that \(p(x)\) is the probability density, which tells us how likely each value \(x\) is. Multiplying \(x\) by \(p(x)\) and integrating gives a probability-weighted average of all possible values, which is why the first moment measures central tendency.

The second moment (\(k=2\)) measures the mean squared value \[ \mu_2 = \mathbb{E}[x^2] = \int x^2 p(x) \mathrm{d}x. \] Combined with the first moment, it gives the variance, the main quantity for uncertainty in machine learning. When the mean is zero, squaring makes positive and negative deviations both contribute positively, so the second moment measures spread. The spread of a distribution relates directly to the precision of our parameter estimates.

Higher moments (\(k > 2\)) are increasingly sensitive to the “tails” of the distribution, the regions far from the center where extreme values occur. As Figure 3.1 shows, raising values to higher powers (\(k\)) amplifies large values much more than small ones. If a value is twice the typical scale, its contribution to the \(k\)th moment is \(2^k\) times that of a typical value. With \(k=3\) it contributes 8 times more, and with \(k=4\) it contributes 16 times more. Because the amplification is exponential in \(k\), even rare extreme values can dominate the higher moments. This makes higher moments useful for studying rare events in astronomy and for testing how sensitive our machine learning models are to outliers.

In the next sections, we study how moments transform, how they relate to marginal and conditional distributions, and how we estimate them from data.

3.2 Transformation of Random Variables

Computing the \(k\)th moment transforms the random variable through \(x \rightarrow x^k\). This is an example of the transformation of random variables, which machine learning uses throughout data preprocessing. Preprocessing means preparing the input variables of a model before fitting it. Machine learning calls these variables features.

As we saw in Chapter 2, \(x\) is an outcome of the random variable \(X\), not a fixed number. A function of a quantity that varies must also vary. So \(x^k\) is an outcome of a new random variable \(X^k\). A function of a random variable is itself a random variable with its own distribution. Preprocessing steps such as taking logarithms or ratios create new random variables whose statistics we need to understand. Standardizing a feature, which means subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation, is another example.

In astronomy we often transform random variables. Examples are converting units (parsecs to light-years), applying calibration corrections, and computing derived quantities such as absolute magnitude from apparent magnitude and distance. To see how a transformation affects a distribution, consider a random variable \(X\) with probability density \(p_X(x)\) and a function \(g\) that defines \(Y = g(X)\). The new variable \(Y\) has its own density \(p_Y(y)\). Given \(p_X(x)\) and \(g\), how do we find \(p_Y(y)\)?

We start with the simplest case, a linear transformation of the form \[ Y = aX + b, \] where \(a\) and \(b\) are constants. The probability densities are then related by \[ p_Y(y) = p_X\left(\frac{y-b}{a}\right)\frac{1}{|a|}. \]

The factor \(1/|a|\) comes from probability conservation. A probability density gives the chance of an outcome per “unit” of the outcome space. As Figure 3.2 illustrates, stretching the distribution by a factor \(a\) (here \(a=2\)) changes what one unit means. Each unit is now \(a\) times larger, so the density per unit must fall by \(1/|a|\) for the total probability to stay equal to one. This factor, which measures how the “unit” changes size, is the Jacobian. It appears whenever we transform between variables, for example when we standardize or rescale features.

For a general transformation \(Y = g(X)\), where \(g\) is differentiable and monotonic (strictly increasing or strictly decreasing), the density transforms as \[ p_Y(y) = p_X(x)\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y}\right| = p_X(g^{-1}(y))\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}g^{-1}(y)\right|. \]The term \(|\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}y|\) is the Jacobian of the transformation. It measures how the transformation stretches or compresses intervals, and it keeps the total probability equal to one. The absolute value keeps the density non-negative when \(g\) is decreasing, because the transformation then reverses the orientation. Probability conservation holds for each small interval, because matching intervals \(\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\mathrm{d}y\) contain the same probability, \(p_X(x)|\mathrm{d}x| = p_Y(y)|\mathrm{d}y|\). Dividing by \(|\mathrm{d}y|\) turns the ratio of the two interval lengths into the derivative \(|\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}y|\).

For a multivariate transformation, the Jacobian becomes a matrix determinant. For a vector of random variables \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, ..., X_D)^T\) that transforms to \(\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{X})\), we have \[ p_Y(\mathbf{y}) = p_X(\mathbf{g}^{-1}(\mathbf{y}))\left|\det\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf{g}^{-1}}{\partial\mathbf{y}}\right)\right|. \]The matrix of partial derivatives \(\partial\mathbf{g}^{-1}/\partial\mathbf{y}\) has element \((i,j)\) equal to \(\partial(\mathbf{g}^{-1})_i/\partial y_j\).

The multivariate case applies when we change coordinate systems (such as equatorial to galactic coordinates) or compute derived quantities from several observables. The choice of coordinates can change how linear a relationship looks, and so it can affect the performance of linear regression.

Another class of transformations combines several random variables, for example in a sum. The sum \(Z = X + Y\) of two random variables is a new random variable. Its distribution depends on the distributions of \(X\) and \(Y\) and on how they relate to each other. This matters in linear regression, where we model the output we want to predict as a linear combination of the inputs. Next, we look at how transformations affect the moments, starting with the expectation.

3.3 Expectation

In the discussion of moments, we introduced the first moment as the mean or expected value of a random variable. This concept is so important that it deserves its own treatment. We now call it the expectation and extend it to functions of \(X\). It involves a weighting, in which each outcome is weighted by its probability, and, for higher moments, a transformation of the variable (\(X \rightarrow X^k\)).

We use probability-weighted averages throughout machine learning, from parameter estimation to loss function optimization (Chapter 4), so we give them their own notation and name. We write the expectation of a random variable \(X\) as \(\mathbb{E}[X]\), defined as \[\begin{aligned} \text{Discrete case:} \quad \mathbb{E}[X] &= \sum_x x \, p_X(x), \\ \text{Continuous case:} \quad \mathbb{E}[X] &= \int x \, p_X(x) \, \mathrm{d}x. \end{aligned}\]The argument inside \(\mathbb{E}[\cdot]\) is the random variable whose expectation we compute. In machine learning we need to distinguish between different averages. In linear regression, for example, we meet the expectation over data points, over the random noise in repeated measurements, and over parameter distributions. Each plays a different role in fitting and uncertainty quantification.

The name “expectation” suggests what we expect to measure, but this can mislead. Consider the Initial Mass Function (IMF) of stars. \(\mathbb{E}[M]\) gives the average stellar mass, but most stars have masses below this value. Stellar masses roughly follow a power law over three orders of magnitude, from the hydrogen-burning limit at 0.08 solar masses to above 100 solar masses. For a Salpeter IMF (\(p(M) \propto M^{-2.35}\)), the density of 0.5 solar mass stars is about 50,000 times that of 50 solar mass stars. The few massive stars still pull the average up, because their large values contribute substantially even though they are rare.

We now see how expectation behaves under the transformations of random variables from the previous section. These properties show how preprocessing steps affect our machine learning models and how to propagate uncertainties through calculations.

For a transformation \(Y = g(X)\), we can compute the expectation in two equivalent ways.

  1. Using the original variable \(X\) and its distribution \[ \mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int g(x) \, p_X(x) \, \mathrm{d}x. \]

  2. Using the transformed variable \(Y\) and its distribution \[ \mathbb{E}[Y] = \int y \, p_Y(y) \, \mathrm{d}y = \int g(x) \, p_X(x) \, \mathrm{d}x. \]

These expressions are equivalent when we account for the transformation of densities with \(p_Y(y) = p_X(g^{-1}(y))|\mathrm{d}g^{-1}/\mathrm{d}y|\). This equivalence is useful in machine learning, where we may transform features before fitting a model. We can compute expected values with either the original or the transformed representation, as long as we handle the probability transformation correctly.

This equivalence is why we can write our definition of moments either way \[ \mu_k = \mathbb{E}[X^k] = \mathbb{E}[Y] \text{ where } Y = X^k. \]

Linearity and Additivity

We now look at the main properties of expectation. For any constants \(a\) and \(b\), expectation is linear \[ \mathbb{E}[aX + b] = a\mathbb{E}[X] + b. \]

Multiplying a random variable by \(a\) stretches or compresses its values by that factor, so the center stretches by \(a\) too. Adding \(b\) shifts the values by that amount, so the center shifts by \(b\), as Figure 3.3 shows. This holds whatever the shape of the distribution, because expectation represents the center of mass of the distribution. In machine learning, linearity tells us how data preprocessing affects model parameters. For example, when we standardize features by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation, linearity shows that the standardized features have zero mean.

Formally, we prove this with the definition of expectation \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[aX + b] &= \int (ax + b)p(x)\mathrm{d}x \\ &= a\int xp(x)\mathrm{d}x + b\int p(x)\mathrm{d}x \\ &= a\mathbb{E}[X] + b, \end{aligned}\] where we used \(\int p(x)\mathrm{d}x = 1\) for any probability distribution.

A subscript names the variables we average over, so \(\mathbb{E}_{X,Y}\) averages over \(X\) and \(Y\) together and \(\mathbb{E}_X\) over \(X\) alone (Section 3.4). For any two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), expectation is additive \[ \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}[X + Y] = \mathbb{E}_X[X] + \mathbb{E}_Y[Y]. \]The expectation of a sum is the sum of the expectations, whether or not \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent (Figure 3.4). Linear regression relies on this, because it models the output as a sum of contributions from different inputs. It follows from \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}[X + Y] &= \iint (x + y)p(x,y)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y \\ &= \iint xp(x,y)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y + \iint yp(x,y)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y \\ &= \int x\left(\int p(x,y)\mathrm{d}y\right)\mathrm{d}x + \int y\left(\int p(x,y)\mathrm{d}x\right)\mathrm{d}y \\ &= \int xp(x)\mathrm{d}x + \int yp(y)\mathrm{d}y \\ &= \mathbb{E}_X[X] + \mathbb{E}_Y[Y], \end{aligned}\] where we used that integrating the joint distribution \(p(x,y)\) over one variable gives the marginal distribution of the other. For example, if we measure the total light from two stars, the average total luminosity is the sum of their average luminosities.

We now extend these ideas to the multivariate setting of most machine learning applications. We represent several random variables as a random vector \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \ldots, X_D)^T\). Its expectation \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}]\) is the vector of the expectations of its components \[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}] \equiv \begin{pmatrix} \mathbb{E}[X_1] \\ \vdots \\ \mathbb{E}[X_D] \end{pmatrix}. \]

When we apply a linear transformation with an \(m \times D\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) to \(\mathbf{X}\), we get a new random vector \(\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{b}\) of dimension \(m\). Expanding the matrix product and using the linearity of expectation gives \[\begin{aligned} Y_i &= \sum_{j=1}^D A_{ij}X_j + b_i, \\ \mathbb{E}[Y_i] &= \sum_{j=1}^D A_{ij}\mathbb{E}[X_j] + b_i. \end{aligned}\]Hence, in the multivariate case \[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Y}] = \mathbf{A}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}] + \mathbf{b}, \] where \(\mathbf{A}\) is an \(m \times D\) transformation matrix and \(\mathbf{b}\) is an \(m\)-dimensional offset vector.

Linearity holds for general linear transformations, in which matrix multiplication mixes the components of \(\mathbf{X}\). Such transformations rotate the coordinate system or create new variables that are linear combinations of the old ones. They are at the heart of linear regression and principal component analysis (Chapter 10).

3.4 Law of Total Expectation

Next, we ask how expectation relates to the marginal and conditional distributions of Chapter 2. This applies when we have only partial information or a hierarchical structure, where the distribution of one variable depends on another.

Suppose we want to estimate a star’s mass, but we can only measure its luminosity directly. We then combine the luminosity measurement with theory about the mass distribution of stars with a given luminosity. This leads to the law of total expectation.

To state the law, we must say which variables we average over. For two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), we use subscripts for this \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}[g(X,Y)] &= \iint g(x,y) \, p(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y, \\ \mathbb{E}_X[g(X,Y)\,|\,Y=y] &= \int g(x,y) \, p(x|y) \, \mathrm{d}x, \end{aligned}\] where the second equation averages only over \(X\) and treats \(Y\) as fixed. It uses the conditional probability \(p(x|y)\), the distribution of \(X\) for a specific value of \(Y\).

This average is the conditional expectation of \(g(X,Y)\) given \(Y=y\). It changes with \(y\), so with \(Y\) left unfixed, \(\mathbb{E}_X[g(X,Y)|Y]\) is itself a random variable.

The law of total expectation says that the overall expectation of \(X\) equals the average, over \(Y\), of its conditional expectations \[ \mathbb{E}_X[X] = \mathbb{E}_Y[\mathbb{E}_X[X|Y]]. \]

To prove this, we write out the right-hand side \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_Y[\mathbb{E}_X[X|Y]] &= \int \mathbb{E}_X[X|Y=y] \, p(y) \, \mathrm{d}y \\ &= \int \left(\int x \, p(x|y) \, \mathrm{d}x\right) p(y) \, \mathrm{d}y \\ &= \int\int x \, p(x|y) \, p(y) \, \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y \\ &= \int\int x \, p(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y \\ &= \int x \left(\int p(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}y\right) \mathrm{d}x \\ &= \int x \, p(x) \, \mathrm{d}x \\ &= \mathbb{E}_X[X], \end{aligned}\] where we used the product rule \(p(x,y) = p(x|y)p(y)\) and the marginal distribution \(p(x) = \int p(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}y\).

The law of total expectation helps when direct measurements are hard or biased. Consider the problem of estimating the average stellar mass, shown in Figure 3.5. The most direct approach averages all stellar masses \[ \mathbb{E}_M[M] = \int M \, p(M) \, \mathrm{d}M. \]

However, we rarely know the true distribution \(p(M)\) in advance, and observational effects such as selection bias make it hard to estimate. In a magnitude-limited survey, for example, we preferentially observe brighter, typically more massive stars. Measuring \(\mathbb{E}_M[M]\) directly requires an accurate sample of the full mass distribution, which observational limits often make impossible.

A better approach uses conditional expectations. We first find the average mass of stars at a given luminosity, then average over all luminosities \[ \mathbb{E}_M[M] = \mathbb{E}_L[\mathbb{E}_M[M|L]] = \int \left(\int M \, p(M|L) \, \mathrm{d}M\right) p(L) \, \mathrm{d}L. \]

As the figure shows, this hierarchical decomposition has practical advantages. For each luminosity (the horizontal dashed lines in the left panel), we compute the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}_M[M|L]\) (the colored circles). The blue contours show the correlation between mass and luminosity. The blue line in the right panel traces how the conditional expectation varies with luminosity. This line is a regression function (Chapter 4) that predicts mass from luminosity.

We then weight these expectations by the luminosity distribution \(p(L)\) (the gray curve in the right panel). We can measure \(p(L)\) directly in our magnitude-limited survey.

This approach handles observational constraints well. We can model the luminosity distribution \(p(L)\) with the selection effects of the survey included, because luminosity relates directly to the survey’s limits. Horizontal slices through the contours in the left panel show the mass distribution at fixed luminosity, \(p(M|L)\). Stellar evolution theory describes it well, and it typically has much smaller observational biases.

As in the univariate case, the law of total expectation extends to random vectors \(\mathbf{X}\) and \(\mathbf{Y}\) \[ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}}[\mathbf{X}] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}}[\mathbf{X}|\mathbf{Y}]]. \]For each component of the random vector, we find the conditional expectation given \(\mathbf{Y}\) and then take the expectation over all values of \(\mathbf{Y}\). The proof follows the univariate steps with extra integration variables, exchanging the order of the multiple integrals over the components of \(\mathbf{X}\) and \(\mathbf{Y}\).

This principle underlies the posterior predictive distribution, the distribution of a new observation given the data, which Section 5.7 develops. In Bayesian analysis, model parameters such as regression coefficients are random variables with uncertainty, and predictions must include that uncertainty. Let \(\theta\) be the model parameters and \(y_*\) a new observation to predict. The law of total expectation gives \[ \mathbb{E}[y_*] = \mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\mathbb{E}[y_*|\theta]]. \]We compute the expected prediction for each parameter value \(\theta\) (the inner expectation), then average over the posterior distribution of \(\theta\) (the outer expectation). This process, called marginalization, includes the parameter uncertainty in our predictions.

3.5 Variance, Covariance, and Correlation

The first moment \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) gives the center of a distribution, but the center alone is not enough. We also need to quantify uncertainty and the relationships between variables. The second moment \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\) seems a reasonable measure of spread, because it weights values far from zero more. But \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\) measures spread only when the distribution is centered at zero. Otherwise it mixes the spread with the location of the center, which makes it unsuitable for uncertainty quantification in most practical cases.

To isolate the spread, we measure deviations from the center \(\mathbb{E}[X]\), not from zero. This defines the variance of a random variable \(X\), written \(\text{Var}[X]\) or \(\sigma^2_X\) \[ \text{Var}[X] \equiv \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2]. \]We first center the distribution by subtracting \(\mathbb{E}[X]\), then average the squared deviation from this center. The variance is the main quantity for prediction uncertainty and for the reliability of parameter estimates. It is the second central moment, meaning a moment about the mean, whereas the moments \(\mu_k\) of Section 3.1 are taken about zero.

We can expand the variance into a more convenient form using the properties of expectation. While \(X\) is a random variable, \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) is a constant (just a number), so linearity applies \[\begin{aligned} \text{Var}[X] &= \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[X^2 - 2X\mathbb{E}[X] + (\mathbb{E}[X])^2] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[X^2] - 2\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[X] + \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[X])^2] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[X^2] - 2(\mathbb{E}[X])^2 + (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 \\ &= \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2. \end{aligned}\]So we can compute the variance from the first and second moments, without computing deviations from the mean directly.

The standard deviation \(\sigma_X\) is the square root of the variance \[ \sigma_X = \sqrt{\text{Var}[X]}. \]

We use the standard deviation because it has the same units as the original variable. If we measure stellar masses in solar masses (\(\mathrm{M}_\odot\)), the variance is in \(\mathrm{M}_\odot^2\) and the standard deviation is in \(\mathrm{M}_\odot\). This makes the standard deviation easier to interpret. If the mean stellar mass is \(1\mathrm{M}_\odot\) with a standard deviation of \(0.5\mathrm{M}_\odot\), we immediately see the scale of the variations.

Next, we look at how variance behaves under transformations, starting with a linear transformation that scales and shifts a random variable. Unlike expectation, which is linear, variance scales differently (Figure 3.6). For any constants \(a\) and \(b\) \[ \text{Var}[aX + b] = a^2\text{Var}[X]. \]

We prove this with the definition of variance and the properties of expectation \[\begin{aligned} \text{Var}[aX + b] &= \mathbb{E}[(aX + b - \mathbb{E}[aX + b])^2] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[(aX + b - (a\mathbb{E}[X] + b))^2] \quad \text{(using linearity of expectation)} \\ &= \mathbb{E}[(aX - a\mathbb{E}[X])^2] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[a^2(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2] \\ &= a^2\mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2] \\ &= a^2\text{Var}[X]. \end{aligned}\]

Multiplying a random variable by \(a\) stretches or compresses the deviations from the mean by \(a\). Variance measures squared deviations, so it scales by \(a^2\). Adding a constant \(b\) shifts the distribution without changing its spread, so it does not change the variance. Scaling variables therefore changes their variance, which affects both interpretation and computation.

Covariance and Correlation

Variance describes the spread of a single variable. Covariance and correlation describe how two variables vary together.

The covariance of two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), written \(\text{Cov}(X,Y)\), measures their joint variability \[ \text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y])]. \]

Covariance measures whether two variables tend to deviate from their means together. When both are above or below their means at the same time, their deviations multiply to positive values, and the covariance is positive. When one is above its mean while the other is below, the products are negative, and so is the covariance. With no linear relationship, positive and negative products cancel, and the covariance is zero.

In astronomical measurements, covariance has two distinct sources. It can come from a physical relationship. For example, more massive stars tend to be more luminous than average, which gives a positive covariance between mass and luminosity. It can also come from the measurement process. Systematic instrument errors that affect several measurements at once create covariance even when the underlying quantities are independent.

Using the properties of expectation, we can write covariance in a more convenient form \[ \text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]. \]

To prove this, we expand the product \[\begin{aligned} \text{Cov}(X,Y) &= \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y])] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[XY - X\mathbb{E}[Y] - Y\mathbb{E}[X] + \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y] + \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]. \end{aligned}\]

Covariance depends on the scale of the variables, which makes it a poor way to compare relationships. To see this, we rescale the variables by constants \(a\) and \(b\) \[\begin{aligned} \text{Cov}(aX, bY) &= \mathbb{E}[(aX - \mathbb{E}[aX])(bY - \mathbb{E}[bY])] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[(aX - a\mathbb{E}[X])(bY - b\mathbb{E}[Y])] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[ab(X - \mathbb{E}[X])(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y])] \\ &= ab\text{Cov}(X,Y). \end{aligned}\]If we change measurement units, for example from solar masses to kilograms (multiplying by \(2 \times 10^{30}\)), the covariance changes in proportion. This makes it hard to compare covariances between different pairs of variables.

To remove this scale dependence, we define the correlation coefficient \[ \rho_{XY} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}, \] which is dimensionless and independent of scale. It lets us compare the strength of relationships between different pairs of variables and see which relationships are strongest in multivariate data. Figure 3.7 shows examples.

We can verify that correlation is scale invariant. For a constant \(a\), variance scales quadratically, with \(\text{Var}[aX] = a^2\text{Var}[X]\). The standard deviation therefore scales as \(\sigma_{aX} = |a|\sigma_X\). Combining this with the scaling of covariance gives \[\begin{aligned} \rho_{aX,bY} &= \frac{\text{Cov}(aX,bY)}{\sigma_{aX}\sigma_{bY}} \\ &= \frac{ab\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{|a|\sigma_X|b|\sigma_Y} \\ &= \text{sign}(ab)\rho_{XY}. \end{aligned}\]Correlation keeps its magnitude under scaling, but its sign depends on the transformation. This is sensible, because multiplying one variable by \(-1\) reverses the direction of the relationship.

Bounds on Correlation

The correlation coefficient lies between \(-1\) and \(+1\). A correlation of \(+1\) means perfect positive correlation, so the variables are linearly related with a positive slope. A correlation of \(-1\) means perfect negative correlation, so one decreases linearly as the other increases. A correlation of zero means no linear relationship. Independent variables have zero correlation, but zero correlation does not make variables independent, because a nonlinear relationship can leave it at zero.

The bound follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. For vectors \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) in an inner product space, it states \[ |\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| \leq \|\mathbf{u}\| \|\mathbf{v}\|, \] where \(\|\cdot\|\) denotes the vector norm.

For random variables, the expectation \(\mathbb{E}[UV]\) plays the role of the inner product of \(U\) and \(V\). For centered random variables, which have their means subtracted, we can show \[\begin{aligned} |\mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y])]| \leq \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2]\mathbb{E}[(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y])^2]}. \end{aligned}\]The left side is the absolute value of the covariance, \(|\text{Cov}(X,Y)|\), and the right side is \(\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)\text{Var}(Y)} = \sigma_X\sigma_Y\). Dividing both sides by \(\sigma_X\sigma_Y\) gives the bound on correlation \[ |\rho_{XY}| = \left|\frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}\right| \leq 1. \]The magnitude of the covariance cannot exceed the product of the standard deviations, which is why correlation lies between \(-1\) and \(1\).

This bound matters in astronomy. A measured correlation tells us how close a linear relationship is to the strongest possible one. The Tully-Fisher relation, for example, shows a strong positive correlation between galaxy luminosity and rotation velocity, close to the maximum possible. This suggests a tight physical link between a galaxy’s light output and its rotation.

Similarly, main sequence stars in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram show a very strong correlation between temperature and luminosity. This correlation reflects the physics of stellar structure, because stars are highly ordered systems governed by precise physical laws.

The Covariance Matrix

For several random variables at once, we use a random vector \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \ldots, X_D)^T\). The variance then generalizes to a covariance matrix, written \(\text{Cov}(\mathbf{X})\) or \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) \[ \text{Cov}(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}])(\mathbf{X} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}])^T]. \]

The transpose matters for the dimensions. \(\mathbf{X} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}]\) is a \(D \times 1\) column vector, and its transpose \((\mathbf{X} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}])^T\) is a \(1 \times D\) row vector. Their product is a \(D \times D\) matrix, in which element \((i,j)\) is the expected product of the deviations of the \(i\)th and \(j\)th components. This gives \[ \Sigma_{ij} = \mathbb{E}[(X_i - \mathbb{E}[X_i])(X_j - \mathbb{E}[X_j])] = \begin{cases} \text{Var}(X_i) & \text{if } i = j \\ \text{Cov}(X_i, X_j) & \text{if } i \neq j \end{cases}. \]The covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) holds all the pairwise covariances between the variables, so it is the basic summary of their linear relationships in multivariate data.

Just as variance scales as \(\text{Var}(aX) = a^2\text{Var}(X)\), the covariance matrix transforms in a fixed way under linear operations. For a linear transformation \(\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{b}\), where \(\mathbf{A}\) is an \(m \times D\) matrix and \(\mathbf{b}\) is an \(m\)-dimensional vector, we have \[ \text{Cov}(\mathbf{Y}) = \mathbf{A}\text{Cov}(\mathbf{X})\mathbf{A}^T. \]This “sandwiching” of the covariance matrix between \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{A}^T\) makes the dimensions work. The \(D \times D\) covariance matrix of \(\mathbf{X}\) becomes an \(m \times m\) covariance matrix for \(\mathbf{Y}\), matching the dimension of the transformed random vector. We prove it with the same properties of expectation as in the univariate case \[\begin{aligned} \text{Cov}(\mathbf{Y}) &= \mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Y}])(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Y}])^T] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{b} - (\mathbf{A}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}] + \mathbf{b}))(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{b} - (\mathbf{A}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}] + \mathbf{b}))^T] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{X} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}])(\mathbf{X} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}])^T\mathbf{A}^T] \\ &= \mathbf{A}\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}])(\mathbf{X} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}])^T]\mathbf{A}^T \\ &= \mathbf{A}\text{Cov}(\mathbf{X})\mathbf{A}^T. \end{aligned}\]

This property has many uses. When we apply principal component analysis (Chapter 10), standardize features, or make another linear transformation, it shows how the covariance structure changes.

3.6 Sampling Statistics and Uncertainty

Next, we ask how variance behaves when we combine different random variables. As with expectation, we start with sums. They arise whenever we combine several observations or propagate errors through a calculation.

For any two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), we have \[ \text{Var}[X + Y] = \text{Var}[X] + 2\text{Cov}(X,Y) + \text{Var}[Y]. \]

We prove this with the definition of variance \[\begin{aligned} \text{Var}[X + Y] &= \mathbb{E}[((X + Y) - \mathbb{E}[X + Y])^2] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[((X - \mathbb{E}[X]) + (Y - \mathbb{E}[Y]))^2] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2 + 2(X - \mathbb{E}[X])(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y]) + (Y - \mathbb{E}[Y])^2] \\ &= \text{Var}[X] + 2\text{Cov}(X,Y) + \text{Var}[Y]. \end{aligned}\]

Unlike expectation, variance does not simply add, because the variance of a sum includes a covariance term. Expanding the squared deviation of \(X + Y\) produces cross terms of the form \((X - \mathbb{E}[X])(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y])\), and their average is the covariance term \(2\text{Cov}(X,Y)\). So the uncertainty of a sum depends on the individual uncertainties and on how the variables move together. This is a basic principle of error propagation in measurements and predictions.

For independent variables, \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0\), and the formula simplifies to \[ \text{Var}[X + Y] = \text{Var}[X] + \text{Var}[Y] \quad \text{(for independent variables)}. \]So the variances of independent random variables add directly (Figure 3.8). This underlies much of statistical analysis and shows how variances add up when we combine measurements or build aggregate statistics.

Uncertainty of the Sample Mean

This additivity gives the uncertainty of a sample mean. In astronomy we often combine several observations of the same quantity to improve precision. Examples are repeated magnitude measurements of a star and repeated spectroscopic observations of a galaxy’s redshift.

Consider \(N\) independent measurements \(\{X_1, ..., X_N\}\) of the same quantity. The sample mean, our best estimate of the true value, is \[ \bar{X} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i. \]

Using the variance properties above, and assuming the measurements are independent with the same variance \(\sigma^2\), we find \[\begin{aligned} \text{Var}[\bar{X}] &= \text{Var}\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i\right] \\ &= \frac{1}{N^2}\text{Var}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i\right] \\ &= \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{i=1}^N \text{Var}[X_i] \quad \text{(all covariances = 0)} \\ &= \frac{1}{N^2}(N\sigma^2) \\ &= \frac{\sigma^2}{N}. \end{aligned}\]This gives the well-known result \[ \text{Var}[\bar{X}] = \frac{\sigma^2}{N}, \] which says that the variance of the mean decreases inversely with sample size. Taking the square root, the uncertainty decreases as \(1/\sqrt{N}\).

This uncertainty, \(\sigma/\sqrt{N}\), is called the standard error of the mean. It is the standard deviation that the sample mean would show over many repeated samples of size \(N\). For large \(N\), the Central Limit Theorem (Section 2.3) also makes the sample mean nearly Gaussian.

If each measurement of a star’s brightness has uncertainty \(\sigma\), averaging \(N\) independent measurements reduces the uncertainty to \(\sigma/\sqrt{N}\) (Figure 3.9). This is why longer exposures, which act like a larger \(N\), give more precise measurements. The same principle explains why larger datasets generally give more reliable parameter estimates. This holds provided the data are independent and identically distributed, meaning the values do not influence each other and share one distribution.

Sampling Noise in Moment Estimates

We return to our original motivation, which is to describe probability distributions with summary statistics. From a finite sample, we estimate moments with sums of the form \[ \hat{\mu}_k = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N x_i^k. \]The hat notation shows that this is an estimate of the true moment \(\mu_k\). Any number computed from a sample, such as \(\hat{\mu}_k\) or \(\bar{X}\), is called a statistic. A rule that turns a sample into an estimate is called an estimator.

The sample covariance of \(N\) pairs \((x_i,y_i)\) is the sum of the products \((x_i - \bar{X})(y_i - \bar{Y})\) of the deviations from the sample means, divided by \(N\). The sample variance is the same expression with \(y_i\) replaced by \(x_i\). Chapters 6 and 10 use these definitions and write \(\mathbb{E}\) for the average over a data set.

The estimate itself varies from sample to sample. This variability is finite sampling noise, the uncertainty from using a finite number of samples to estimate properties of the underlying population. The population is the full distribution from which the sample is drawn. This noise determines how reliable our parameter estimates and inferences are.

Consider estimating the moments of the stellar IMF. Even with perfect mass measurements, \(\hat{\mu}_k\) would vary if we repeated the measurement with different random samples of stars. Each star’s mass is a random draw from the IMF, so \(X^k\) and therefore \(\hat{\mu}_k\) are random variables. In general, even with perfect measurements, estimates carry uncertainty because they come from finite samples. We must estimate this uncertainty for reliable inference.

As we found for sample means, moment estimates become more precise with larger samples. For independent measurements, the variance of the \(k\)th moment estimate scales as \(\text{Var}(X^k)/N\), so the sampling noise decreases as \(1/\sqrt{N}\). This is one reason modern astronomy carries out deep surveys with wide sky coverage. The large number of objects reduces finite sampling noise, which gives more precise estimates of population statistics and tighter constraints on theoretical models.

The \(1/\sqrt{N}\) scaling gives the expected improvement with sample size. The total uncertainty also depends on \(\text{Var}(X^k)\), whose size relative to \(\mu^{2k}\) grows rapidly with \(k\). To see why, expand a fluctuation around the mean. If \(X = \mu + \delta\), where \(\mu\) is the mean of \(X\), a Taylor expansion gives \[\begin{aligned} X^k &= (\mu + \delta)^k \\ &= \mu^k + k\mu^{k-1}\delta + \frac{k(k-1)}{2}\mu^{k-2}\delta^2 + \ldots. \end{aligned}\]

If we keep only the linear term \(\mu^k + k\mu^{k-1}\delta\), the scaling property of variance gives \[ \text{Var}(X^k) \approx k^2\mu^{2k-2}\text{Var}(X). \]Relative to \(\mu^{2k}\), this variance is \(k^2\,\text{Var}(X)/\mu^2\), so it grows approximately as \(k^2\). As in our earlier discussion of higher moments, astronomical distributions often contain a few very massive galaxies or extremely bright quasars. These objects have a large effect on higher-moment estimates, so those estimates are noisier than lower-moment estimates. The same happens in other fields with heavy-tailed distributions.

Yet higher moments often carry the physical information we want. In cosmology, for example, the non-Gaussian features of the galaxy distribution, which appear only in moments beyond the variance, constrain theories of structure formation. This sets up a trade-off. Higher moments carry unique physical information, but they need much larger samples to measure well. We must balance information content against estimation precision when we design studies and analyze data.

3.7 Bootstrapping

The \(1/\sqrt{N}\) scaling law shows how uncertainty decreases with sample size, but in practice we often need precise values for the uncertainties. Our analysis of \(\text{Var}(X^k)\) kept only the leading term of the Taylor expansion, to build intuition. The neglected higher-order terms can matter, especially for small samples or highly skewed distributions, which are common in astronomy.

For multidimensional or nonlinear statistics, analytical expressions can become intractable. This leads us to empirical methods for estimating uncertainty, which have grown in importance with computational statistics.

The bootstrap estimates the variance of an estimator when analytical expressions are not available (Figure 3.10). Given an original sample \(\{x_1, \ldots, x_N\}\), the algorithm is

  1. Draw \(N\) values from this set with replacement, so each value can be drawn again. They form a “bootstrap sample” \(\{x_1^*, \ldots, x_N^*\}\)

  2. Calculate the statistic of interest, for example the \(k\)th moment, on this bootstrap sample \[ \hat{\mu}_k^* = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i^*)^k \]

  3. Repeat steps 1 and 2 many times (typically thousands)

  4. Use the variance of these bootstrap estimates to approximate \(\text{Var}(\hat{\mu}_k)\)

For example, if the original dataset is \(\{1, 2, 3\}\), one bootstrap sample might be \(\{1, 1, 2\}\) and another \(\{2, 3, 3\}\). Each bootstrap sample has the same size as the original, but some values appear more than once and others not at all. This resampling mimics the variability we would see if we could collect new datasets of the same size from the same population. It gives a computational solution to what is otherwise a theoretical problem.

Why the Bootstrap Works

The logic of the bootstrap comes from how we think about sampling. Our sample \(\{x_1, ..., x_N\}\) is drawn from an unknown probability distribution \(p(x)\). If we knew \(p(x)\), a moment would just be an integral, as above. We usually have only a finite sample. The bootstrap uses this sample as a stand-in for the underlying distribution. We can then study the sampling distribution of our statistics, meaning how they vary from sample to sample.

Resampling with replacement treats the observed sample as a discrete approximation to \(p(x)\), called the empirical distribution, in which each observed value has probability \(1/N\). Our original sample was drawn from the true distribution \(p(x)\), and the bootstrap samples are drawn from this empirical distribution. If we could draw many new samples from \(p(x)\), we could study how \(\hat{\mu}_k\) varies between them. That would show its sampling distribution and its uncertainty. The bootstrap approximates this ideal process using only the data we have, so it needs no additional data collection.

As the sample size \(N\) grows, the empirical distribution approaches the true distribution \(p(x)\). The distribution of bootstrap statistics then approaches the true sampling distribution. This is why the bootstrap gives reliable estimates of sampling uncertainty and why we use it widely for model validation (Section 4.7) and uncertainty quantification.

The strength of the bootstrap is its generality. Instead of deriving analytical formulas for standard errors, which may be intractable for complex statistics, we get the sampling behavior directly by simulation. It suits astronomy, where we often need the uncertainty of complex measurements such as galaxy morphology classifications or stellar parameters from spectroscopy. It also applies in other fields with complex statistics, from economics to ecology. There it gives uncertainties for quantities from correlation coefficients to diversity indices, which measure the variety of species in a sample.

When the Bootstrap Fails

The bootstrap can fail in three ways.

First, the sample must be representative. The bootstrap assumes the sample is large enough to approximate the underlying distribution. If it misses features of \(p(x)\), such as rare events, the bootstrap misses them too. This applies most to higher moments, which are sensitive to the tails. It also applies to applications that focus on the tails. Examples are extreme value analysis, which studies the largest values of a sample, and risk assessment.

Second, the basic bootstrap resamples individual values and so treats observations as independent. This can mislead when data are correlated, as in time series or spatial data where neighboring measurements are related. In astronomy this can happen for galaxy clustering or stellar variability. Block bootstrapping was designed for this case. It resamples blocks of observations, which preserves the correlation within each block.

Third, for statistics that depend on extreme values, the bootstrap can underestimate uncertainty. It can only resample values that are in the original sample, so it cannot produce new extreme values that future datasets might contain. The uncertainty estimates for statistics that are sensitive to outliers can then be too optimistic. This matters in hydrology and finance, where extreme events carry great importance.

Even so, the bootstrap is among our most useful tools for estimating uncertainty. Its logic is simple, and it suits astronomical measurements that are complex and have unknown underlying distributions. Two related methods exist. Parametric bootstrapping resamples from a fitted parametric distribution instead of the empirical distribution. The jackknife leaves out one observation at a time to measure its influence on the statistic.

3.8 Law of Total Variance

Just as the law of total expectation breaks down expected values in hierarchical problems, the law of total variance decomposes variability. It shows how much of our uncertainty comes from different sources, such as measurement noise and intrinsic variability, or explainable and unexplainable variation.

For any two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), the law of total variance states \[ \text{Var}_X[X] = \mathbb{E}_Y[\text{Var}_X[X|Y]] + \text{Var}_Y[\mathbb{E}_X[X|Y]]. \]

The total variance of a random variable splits into two parts with clear meanings. The first term, \(\mathbb{E}_Y[\text{Var}_X[X|Y]]\), is the expected conditional variance, the average “unexplained” variability that remains after we know \(Y\). For each value of \(Y\), the conditional variance is the spread of possible \(X\) values, and we average these spreads over all values of \(Y\). For example, even if we know a star’s luminosity (\(Y\)) exactly, its mass (\(X\)) is still uncertain. Stars of the same luminosity can differ slightly in mass because of factors like age and metallicity. This term gives that remaining uncertainty, averaged over all luminosities, which is irreducible once we use all our information about \(Y\).

The second term, \(\text{Var}_Y[\mathbb{E}_X[X|Y]]\), is the variability of \(X\) that knowing \(Y\) explains. It measures how much the average value of \(X\) changes as \(Y\) changes. In our stellar example, it measures how much the average stellar mass varies with luminosity, which is the strength of the mass-luminosity relation itself. It is the part of the variance that the relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\) explains.

Proof of the Law

To prove the law, we write the total variance and split the deviation \((X - \mathbb{E}_X[X])\) into two parts. One is the deviation from the conditional mean, \((X - \mathbb{E}_X[X|Y])\). The other is the deviation of the conditional mean from the overall mean, \((\mathbb{E}_X[X|Y] - \mathbb{E}_X[X])\) \[\begin{aligned} \text{Var}_X[X] &= \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[((X - \mathbb{E}[X|Y]) + (\mathbb{E}[X|Y] - \mathbb{E}[X]))^2] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X|Y])^2] + \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[X|Y] - \mathbb{E}[X])^2] \\ &\quad + 2\mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X|Y])(\mathbb{E}[X|Y] - \mathbb{E}[X])]. \end{aligned}\]

The cross term vanishes because \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X|Y])(\mathbb{E}[X|Y] - \mathbb{E}[X])] &= \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X|Y])(\mathbb{E}[X|Y] - \mathbb{E}[X])|Y]] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[X|Y] - \mathbb{E}[X])\mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X|Y])|Y]] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[X|Y] - \mathbb{E}[X]) \cdot 0] \\ &= 0, \end{aligned}\] where the first step applies the law of total expectation (Section 3.4) to the product. The second step moves the factor \(\mathbb{E}[X|Y] - \mathbb{E}[X]\) outside the inner expectation, because it is a fixed number once \(Y\) is given. The third step uses \(\mathbb{E}[X - \mathbb{E}[X|Y]\,|\,Y] = 0\), because given \(Y\) the deviation of \(X\) from its average \(\mathbb{E}[X|Y]\) averages to zero.

The remaining terms give \[\begin{aligned} \text{Var}_X[X] &= \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X|Y])^2] + \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[X|Y] - \mathbb{E}[X])^2] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X|Y])^2|Y]] + \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[X|Y] - \mathbb{E}[X])^2] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}[X|Y]] + \text{Var}[\mathbb{E}[X|Y]], \end{aligned}\] which is exactly the law of total variance. The second line applies the law of total expectation to the first term. The inner expectation in the second line is the conditional variance \(\text{Var}[X|Y]\). The second term is \(\text{Var}[\mathbb{E}[X|Y]]\) because \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X|Y]] = \mathbb{E}[X]\) by the same law.

Interpretation and Extensions

Figure 3.11 illustrates this decomposition with the stellar mass-luminosity relationship. Individual stars are blue points, which show how masses vary at each luminosity. The red line traces the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}_M[M|L]\), the average mass of stars at each luminosity. The red shaded region shows the conditional spread at each luminosity, which is how much stellar masses typically differ from this average. At \(\log(L/\mathrm{L}_\odot) = 0.5\) (the blue box), we see the spread of masses around the conditional mean. Averaging these conditional variances over all luminosities, weighted by how common each luminosity is, gives the first term, \(\mathbb{E}_L[\text{Var}_M[M|L]]\).

The green shaded region on the right side of the figure shows the second term. It shows how much the conditional expectations themselves change with luminosity. This variation of \(\mathbb{E}_M[M|L]\) (the red line) with \(L\) is \(\text{Var}_L[\mathbb{E}_M[M|L]]\). It is the part of the total mass variance that the mass-luminosity relationship explains.

Better measurements reduce only the measurement-noise part of the first term. If intrinsic scatter at fixed \(Y\) makes up most of that term, or if the second term dominates, the total uncertainty barely changes. In stellar spectroscopy, for example, better resolution or signal-to-noise ratio stops helping beyond a certain point. This happens if the remaining variation comes from intrinsic stellar variability and differences between stellar populations. This matters for experimental design and for how we spend our resources.

The decomposition also shows when an extra variable helps prediction. If the expected conditional variance \(\mathbb{E}_Y[\text{Var}_X[X|Y]]\) is much smaller than \(\text{Var}_X[X]\), knowing \(Y\) greatly reduces our uncertainty about \(X\), so \(Y\) is a useful predictor. If the two variances are similar, \(Y\) gives little predictive information about \(X\). It helps us judge how useful different variables are for prediction.

The law of total variance generalizes to the multivariate case \[ \text{Cov}(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Cov}(\mathbf{X}|\mathbf{Y})] + \text{Cov}(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}|\mathbf{Y}]). \]The same proof applies, because it used only properties of expectation that hold for vectors. The interpretation is similar. The total covariance is the average of the conditional covariances plus the covariance of the conditional means. This applies to systems of several variables, such as multivariate regression or physical systems with several interacting components.

The law of total variance also applies to predictive uncertainty in Bayesian statistics. Model parameters such as regression coefficients are random variables with uncertainty. To predict a new outcome \(y_*\) while including this parameter uncertainty, the law of total variance splits the predictive variance \[ \text{Var}[y_*] = \mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\text{Var}[y_*|\theta]] + \text{Var}_{\theta}[\mathbb{E}[y_*|\theta]]. \]The first term is the average variance of the predictions at each parameter value \(\theta\), weighted by the posterior distribution of \(\theta\). The second term is how much our predictions vary because of parameter uncertainty. These two terms are the aleatoric uncertainty, the randomness left when the parameters are known, and the epistemic uncertainty, our limited knowledge of them.

We can now describe a distribution with a few summary statistics, track how their uncertainty shrinks with sample size, and split variability into its sources. The next two chapters use expectations, variances, and covariances to fit a linear regression and to find the uncertainty of its parameters.

3.9 Tutorial: Finding Baryon Acoustic Oscillations

This tutorial applies the covariance and the bootstrap of this chapter to a faint signal in the galaxy distribution, the baryon acoustic oscillation. Cosmologists use it to measure how the universe expanded. The full tutorial can be found at https://statml.org/ as tutorial 3.

In the first 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe was a hot plasma of ordinary matter, called baryons, and light. Sound waves moved through it. When atoms formed, the waves froze in place after traveling about 150 million parsecs (in today’s units). This left galaxies slightly more likely to be that far apart. This separation is a standard ruler, a length that we know. Its apparent size at each epoch gives the distance to the galaxies, and so how the universe expanded. The signal is faint, because the excess of galaxy pairs at this separation is small.

To find such a faint signal, we must first decide what to measure. We observe one universe, which is one random sample from the distribution that theory predicts. The positions of galaxies are therefore random variables, and a map is a finite sample. Theory does not predict where each galaxy sits. It predicts statistical properties, such as how galaxy pairs are correlated at each separation. The data must therefore be compressed into summary statistics, each with a sampling uncertainty.

The first candidates are the mean and the variance, the moments of Section 3.1. To test them, the tutorial simulates a toy universe, a map with a ring of radius \(R\) in random noise (Figure 3.12a). The ring stands for the preferred separation and takes its brightness from the background, as the real signal moves galaxies and does not create them. The mean and the variance of the map therefore do not change, so these two statistics do not reveal the ring. Shuffling the pixels would leave them unchanged and would destroy the ring.

A statistic that shows the ring must depend on where the pixels lie. The covariance of Section 3.5 does, because it compares pairs of pixels. Pixels on the ring are brighter than average, so pairs of them have a positive covariance. Plotted against the separation of the two pixels, this covariance is what astronomers call the correlation function (Figure 3.12b). Two points on a ring are at most a diameter \(2R\) apart, and most often close to it. The covariance therefore rises toward \(2R\) and drops quickly beyond it. Pairs close together on the ring also give a high covariance at small separations.

Whether this feature is real depends on its sampling uncertainty (Section 3.6). We observe the universe once, so the bootstrap of Section 3.7 uses the sample itself to estimate how the statistic would vary. The drop beyond \(2R\) is much larger than the resulting error bars, and maps without a ring show no such feature (Figure 3.12b).

The same reasoning applies to a real survey. A galaxy survey measures the ruler from a similar bump in the correlation function of galaxy positions. The real signal is much weaker than our ring, so surveys need very large volumes to make the sampling noise small.

Theory predicts a summary statistic, the data estimate it from one finite sample, and the bootstrap tells us how far to trust the estimate. The covariance of pairs depends on where things lie and the mean and variance do not, so the statistic must match the signal. The same recipe applies to characteristic scales in noisy spatial data.

Further Reading

Fisher (1922) developed the ideas of efficiency, sufficiency and consistency that remain central to statistical inference. Cramér (1946) gave a mathematical treatment that connects probability theory with statistical methods. Cox and Hinkley (1974) emphasize the general concepts of statistical theory. Casella and Berger (2002) is a graduate text that derives statistical inference from probability. Kendall and Stuart (1977) and Stuart and Ord (1994) are editions of an extensive reference on distribution theory and the properties of moments. Taylor (1982) is a widely used introduction to error analysis and the propagation of uncertainty. Efron (1979) developed the bootstrap, and Davison and Hinkley (1997) cover its theory and applications. Lupton (1993) explains classical statistical theory for scientists. Wall and Jenkins (2003) cover statistical methods for observational astronomy, both frequentist and Bayesian.
